newsitem.title: USA: U.S. stocks put positive spin on jobs data.
newsitem.headline: U.S. stocks put positive spin on jobs data.

text.p: U.S. stocks put a positive spin on a stronger-than-expected U.S. December employment report on Friday, seeing it as a signal of a strong economy that will ease recent fears of weakening corporate profits.
The report caused carnage in the inflation-wary Treasuries market but, after initially stumbling, U.S. blue chips powered back into record territory.

"If the economy proves to be somewhat stronger than most people think...then you're going to have very good earnings growth," said Stan Shipley, senior strategist at Lehman Brothers, after the release of the December payrolls data.

Before the stock market's opening on Friday the Labor Department said December non-farm payrolls rose 262,000. Economists had forecasted about 190,000 new jobs in December. Wages also topped expectations, rising 0.5 percent versus forecasts for a 0.2 percent increase.
The Dow industrials sank 67 points in the first half-hour of trading, triggered by a sharp selloff in the bond market.

But unlike Treasuries, stocks recovered strongly later in the day. The Dow industrials were up about 62 points in afternoon trading to 6687, while the Nasdaq composite gained rose over four points at 1331.
The 30-year bond was down 1-11/32 to yield 6.86 percent.

Bruce Bittles, market strategist at J.C. Bradford, noted that late last year there were fears in the stock market that an economic slowdown would bring a "recession" in U.S. corporate earnings in 1997.
The jobs data "takes away the recession fears and certainly should help corporate earnings," Bittles said.
Driving the recovery in stocks was bargain hunting and money from institutional investors needing to take positions at the start of the year, analysts said.

They also said money could be flowing into Wall Street stocks from investors fleeing Japan's battered markets, where Tokyo's Nikkei index lost almost 11 percent in the first week of trading in the New Year.
Market analysts said they did not expect the December jobs data to trigger a Federal Reserve rate hike, an ever-present concern for both stocks and bonds.
In a Reuter poll, 27 of 29 economists surveyed Friday projected no change in the federal funds rate or the discount rate at the next Federal Open Market Committee meeting on February 4-5.
But they cautioned that a continued rise in interest rates in the bond market could eventually trip up stocks, partly by drawing investors out of stocks and into bonds.
"If interest rates continue to (rise) rapidly, I think you have to call the bullish thesis into question," said Robert von Pentz, a managing partner at Columbia Partners.

"Perhaps the worst thing that could happen is that interest rates move higher as the flow into the market deteriorates in the spring," Pentz added. "That sets us up for another poor summer like we had last summer."
The Dow lost about three percent last July.
